Licensure vs certification vs accreditation as three distinct concepts

claims.claim: U.S. healthcare is regulated at three levels simultaneously: federal (e.g., CMS Conditions of Participation, FDA, OIG fraud enforcement, OSHA, EMTALA), state (facility and professional licensure, scope of practice, certificate of need), and voluntary private accreditation.

Licensure (mandatory state permission to operate or practice), certification (meeting federal Conditions of Participation to be paid by Medicare/Medicaid), and accreditation (voluntary review by a private organization against its own standards) are three distinct concepts.

Statutes (laws from Congress) sit above agency regulations, which are issued through notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. 553) and carry the force of law; sub-regulatory guidance such as CMS manuals interprets regulations, is used operationally, but does not have the force of law, and the regulation controls in a conflict.

Under Section 1865 of the Social Security Act, accreditation by a CMS-approved accrediting organization can be 'deemed' to show compliance with the Conditions of Participation, so the accreditation survey substitutes for the state survey agency's compliance survey; providers still must meet the CoPs and CMS conducts validation surveys on a sample.

Enforcement is survey-driven: surveys against the CoPs find deficiencies, the provider must submit and implement a plan of correction, and the ultimate federal sanction for uncorrected condition-level noncompliance is termination of the Medicare provider agreement (42 CFR Part 488).

The Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7b(b)) is a criminal, intent-based prohibition on paying to induce referrals, while the physician self-referral law (Stark Law, 42 U.S.C. 1395nn) is a strict-liability civil law barring physician referrals to entities with which the physician has a financial relationship, regardless of intent; OIG enforces exclusions from federal programs.

EMTALA (42 U.S.C. 1395dd) requires Medicare-participating hospitals with emergency departments to provide an appropriate medical screening examination and to stabilize emergency medical conditions (or arrange an appropriate transfer), regardless of a patient's ability to pay.

The FDA regulates the marketing of drugs and medical devices under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act; devices are regulated on a risk-based classification (Class I, II, III) with premarket pathways including 510(k) clearance and premarket approval (PMA).

As of January 2025, 35 states and the District of Columbia operated certificate-of-need (CON) programs, which require state approval before certain major capital expenditures or new services and aim to limit duplication and control costs; CON is therefore a state-level regulatory tool that does not exist everywhere.

The hospital Conditions of Participation (42 CFR Part 482) require, among other things, an effective governing body legally responsible for the hospital and an organized medical staff, illustrating that CoPs are federal regulations, not statutes or guidance.

sourceRecords.title: 42 CFR Part 482 — Conditions of Participation for Hospitals (482.12 Governing body; 482.22 Medical staff)
sourceRecords.provider: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (National Archives / GPO)
sourceRecords.notes: Reused from the source registry. Used as the primary example that Conditions of Participation are federal regulations (not statutes or guidance) and to anchor the certification concept: hospitals must meet these CoPs to participate in Medicare. Supports the governance/medical-staff illustration and the statute-vs-regulation hierarchy.

sourceRecords.title: 42 CFR Part 488 — Survey, Certification, and Enforcement Procedures
sourceRecords.provider: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (National Archives / GPO)
sourceRecords.notes: Structure confirmed via the eCFR versioner API (title-42 structure JSON) because the eCFR HTML redirected the fetcher. Sections used: 488.2 statutory basis; 488.4 general rules for a CMS-approved accreditation program; 488.5 application by national accrediting organizations; 488.7 release and use of accreditation surveys; 488.9 validation surveys; 488.11 state survey agency functions; 488.13 loss of accreditation; 488.456/488.604/488.865/488.1265 termination of provider agreement; 488.424 directed plan of correction. Supports deemed status, validation surveys, plans of correction, and termination as the enforcement endpoint.

sourceRecords.title: 42 U.S.C. 1395dd — Examination and treatment for emergency medical conditions and women in labor (EMTALA)

sourceRecords.title: Fraud & Abuse Laws (Physician Education) — False Claims Act, Anti-Kickback Statute, Physician Self-Referral (Stark) Law, Exclusion Statute, Civil Monetary Penalties Law
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (OIG)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch of the OIG page. Supports the citations and the key distinction: Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7b(b)) is criminal and intent-based; the physician self-referral (Stark) law (42 U.S.C. 1395nn) is a strict-liability civil law requiring no proof of intent; also the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. 3729-3733), Exclusion Statute (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7), and Civil Monetary Penalties Law (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7a). Used at a naming level, per anti-duplication scope.

sourceRecords.title: Accrediting Organizations (AOs) and deeming authority (Section 1865 of the Social Security Act)
sourceRecords.notes: The CMS host returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher (a documented behavior for cms.gov), so deemed-status details were verified via web-search excerpts of CMS pages and corroborated by 42 CFR Part 488. Supports that Section 1865 of the Social Security Act authorizes CMS to grant deeming authority to national accrediting organizations whose standards meet or exceed Medicare's, so their accreditation can substitute for the state agency compliance survey, subject to CMS validation surveys. Named accreditors (e.g., The Joint Commission, DNV) referenced only; no standards text used. Recorded REFERENCE_ONLY because the canonical page could not be fetched directly.

sourceRecords.title: 5 U.S.C. 553 — Rule making (Administrative Procedure Act)
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives (United States Code)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch of the canonical uscode.house.gov page. Supports the notice-and-comment rulemaking process: agencies publish a general notice of proposed rule making in the Federal Register, give interested persons an opportunity to comment, and incorporate a concise general statement of basis and purpose, with substantive rules generally effective not less than 30 days after publication. Anchors the statute-vs-regulation distinction.
